"All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement said. The finance minister's assistant told CNN that Manuel is willing to serve in the new government, if needed. Three deputy ministers have also tendered their resignations, a government statement said. Motlanthe will stay in office until elections in the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely expected to win. Earlier this month, the ANC asked Mbeki to step down after a judge threw out the corruption, fraud and racketeering case against Zuma -- Mbeki's political arch rival. The judge called the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference. Mbeki -- who has been South Africa's president for nearly 10 years -- spoke of some of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation on Sunday during a televised address.  Watch the significance of Mbeki "falling on the sword" » . "I depart this office knowing that many men and woman in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. Mbeki said the country still has economic, corruption and crime challenges to face in the future. And he gave his vote of confidence to the country's next leader without naming who that leader would be. Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced Saturday that the party -- which Mbeki has been involved with since his teens -- had asked him to leave before his term was up. Mbeki agreed to do so, he said. He said the case was politically motivated, and harmed his chances to become the ANC's presidential nominee. He could have faced at least 15 years in jail if convicted of accepting bribes from a company that got a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal. He also faced charges of having a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes for Zuma and using Zuma's political influence to benefit his businesses. Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics alleged he pushed for the corruption charges against Zuma. Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing deal between Zimbabwe's political rivals, who signed the agreement on Monday in an effort to put aside the violent past and end the crisis that has paralyzed Zimbabwe since disputed national elections in March. Under it, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe remains president, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, has become prime minister and the coordinator of government affairs.

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN) -- Ten South African ministers and the deputy president have tendered their resignations as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to depart from office.

South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation in a televised address on Sunday. His successor, African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe, will be sworn in as South Africa's president on Thursday.

Mbeki's announcement on Sunday prompted several Cabinet members to threaten resignation in solidarity; however, the outgoing president urged them to remain in their posts, government sources said. The resignations—which include those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—will take effect Thursday, when Mbeki formally steps down, according to a government statement.

"All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement read. The finance minister's assistant told CNN that Manuel remains willing to serve in the new government, should he be required to do so.

Three deputy ministers have likewise submitted their resignations, a government statement confirmed.

A spokesman for South Africa's ruling party, the African National Congress, confirmed that it has selected Motlanthe as its choice to succeed Mbeki. Motlanthe is expected to serve until the elections scheduled for the spring of next year, which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely anticipated to win.

Earlier this month, the ANC called on Mbeki to step down after a judge dismissed the corruption, fraud, and racketeering case against Zuma—Mbeki's chief political rival. The judge deemed the case invalid and accused Mbeki's government of political interference.

Mbeki—who has served as South Africa's president for nearly a decade—reflected on several of his achievements when he formally announced his resignation during Sunday's televised address.

Watch the significance of Mbeki "falling on the sword" »

"I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," Mbeki said. Under his leadership, he noted, the country experienced the longest period of sustained economic growth in its history and extended assistance to its most impoverished citizens in an unprecedented manner.

Mbeki acknowledged, however, that the nation continues to face significant challenges in the areas of economic development, corruption, and crime. He also offered his vote of confidence to the country's next leader, though he refrained from naming that individual.

Gwede Mantashe, secretary-general of the African National Congress, announced on Saturday that the party—with which Mbeki has been affiliated since his teenage years—had requested that he step down before the conclusion of his term. Mbeki, he said, agreed to comply.

Mantashe explained that the ANC reached this decision "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country," and to ensure that the ANC movement remained "stable and unified."

The case against Zuma—who succeeded Mbeki as ANC president last year—was initially dismissed in September 2006, but the National Prosecuting Authority subsequently reinstated the charges. Judge Chris Nicholson issued no ruling on Zuma's guilt or innocence, leaving open the possibility that he could be charged once more. Political observers, however, considered such an outcome unlikely, given Zuma's considerable popularity, particularly among the Communist Party and the trade unions.

Zuma has denied all charges, asserting that the case was politically motivated and had damaged his prospects of becoming the ANC's presidential nominee. Had he been convicted of accepting bribes from a company that secured a contract in a multibillion-dollar arms deal, he could have faced a minimum of 15 years in prison. He also faced charges of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is currently serving a 15-year sentence for soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf and exploiting Zuma's political influence to benefit his own business interests.

Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics have alleged that he pressed for the corruption charges against Zuma.

Mbeki recently brokered a power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe's rival political factions, who signed the accord on Monday in an effort to move beyond a violent past and resolve the crisis that has crippled Zimbabwe since the disputed national elections in March. Under the terms of the agreement, longtime Zimbabwean leader Robert Mugabe retains the presidency, while his perennial rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister and coordinator of government affairs.

In a dramatic turn of events that has reshaped South Africa's political landscape, President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation during a televised address to the nation. The decision came after the African National Congress (ANC), the country's dominant political party, formally requested that he step down from office.

The resignation was precipitated by a judge's dismissal of corruption charges against Jacob Zuma, Mbeki's longtime political rival within the party. The court's ruling not only cleared Zuma of the allegations but also raised troubling questions about whether the prosecution had been politically motivated—concerns that placed significant pressure on Mbeki's position and ultimately led the ANC leadership to conclude that his continued presidency was no longer tenable.

The political upheaval did not end with Mbeki's announcement. In the aftermath of his resignation, ten cabinet ministers, along with the deputy president, offered to step down from their positions as well, signaling the depth of the divisions within the government and the far-reaching consequences of this leadership crisis.

To fill the void left by Mbeki's departure, ANC Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe is set to be sworn in as the new head of state on Thursday. Motlanthe will serve in a caretaker capacity, guiding the country until the national elections scheduled for the spring. Political observers widely anticipate that Jacob Zuma will emerge victorious in those elections, positioning him to assume the presidency in his own right.

This transition marks the end of an era for South Africa. Mbeki had led the nation for nearly a decade, and his departure represents one of the most significant political shifts the country has experienced since the end of apartheid. As South Africa navigates this period of transition, the events surrounding Mbeki's resignation underscore the intense internal dynamics of the ANC and the evolving nature of power within the nation's governing party.

# Johannesburg: The Heart of South Africa

Johannesburg, often affectionately called "Joburg" or "Jozi" by locals, stands as the largest city in South Africa and one of the most dynamic urban centers on the African continent. Located in the northeastern part of the country, this vibrant metropolis serves as the economic powerhouse of the nation.

## A City Born from Gold

Johannesburg's origins are deeply rooted in the discovery of gold in 1886. What began as a small mining settlement rapidly transformed into a bustling city as prospectors and fortune seekers flocked to the region. This golden legacy earned the city its nickname "eGoli," meaning "place of gold" in local languages. Today, evidence of this rich mining history remains visible throughout the urban landscape.

## Economic Significance

As the commercial and financial capital of South Africa, Johannesburg drives much of the country's economy. The city is home to the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, the largest stock exchange in Africa, and serves as headquarters for numerous multinational corporations. Its thriving business districts attract entrepreneurs, professionals, and investors from around the world.

## Cultural Diversity

Johannesburg is a melting pot of cultures, languages, and traditions. People from various ethnic backgrounds and different parts of Africa call this city home, creating a rich tapestry of cultural experiences. This diversity is reflected in the city's cuisine, music, art, and festivals.

## Historical Landmarks

The city holds profound historical importance, particularly in the story of South Africa's journey through apartheid and its transition to democracy. Nearby Soweto township played a pivotal role in the anti-apartheid struggle. The Apartheid Museum and the Nelson Mandela sites offer visitors powerful insights into the nation's complex past.

## Conclusion

Johannesburg embodies the spirit of modern South Africa—resilient, diverse, and constantly evolving. From its golden beginnings to its status as a global city, Johannesburg continues to shine as a beacon of opportunity and progress on the African continent.

**Pretoria, South Africa** — South African President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation on Sunday, bowing to pressure from the ruling African National Congress (ANC) party that had asked him to step down before the end of his term.

Mbeki, 66, addressed the nation in a televised speech, stating he would leave office after the ANC's National Executive Committee formally requested his recall. His departure marks a dramatic end to nearly a decade of leadership in Africa's largest economy.

"I have been a loyal member of the African National Congress for 52 years," Mbeki said in his address. "I remain a member of the ANC and therefore will always abide by its decisions."

## Political Rift Behind the Resignation

The move came days after a High Court judge suggested there may have been political interference in the corruption case against Jacob Zuma, Mbeki's rival and the current ANC president. The judgment fueled long-simmering tensions between the two men and their factions within the party.

Zuma had defeated Mbeki for the ANC presidency in December, setting up a power struggle that ultimately led to Sunday's dramatic developments. Supporters of Zuma had accused Mbeki of orchestrating legal proceedings to derail Zuma's political ambitions—allegations Mbeki has denied.

## Cabinet Ministers Follow With Resignations

In the wake of Mbeki's departure, several senior cabinet ministers announced they too would step down, raising concerns about political stability and economic uncertainty.

Among those who resigned was Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, a figure widely respected by international markets and credited with steering South Africa's economy through years of steady growth. Manuel's decision initially sent ripples of anxiety through financial markets, though officials later clarified he would be available to serve in the new administration.

Other ministers who tendered their resignations in solidarity with Mbeki included several key members of his administration, signaling the depth of the political realignment underway within the government.

## Transition of Power

Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe was widely expected to serve as interim leader until national elections scheduled for the following year. The ANC moved quickly to reassure both citizens and international observers that the transition would be orderly and constitutional.

Party officials emphasized that the changes represented an internal political matter and that South Africa's democratic institutions remained strong and intact.

## A Legacy of Mixed Reviews

Mbeki, who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999, leaves behind a complicated legacy. He was praised for overseeing economic growth and playing a role in African diplomatic efforts, including mediation in regional conflicts.

However, his tenure was also marked by criticism over his handling of the HIV/AIDS crisis and his approach to the political situation in neighboring Zimbabwe.

## Looking Ahead

Analysts said the political drama underscored the maturity of South Africa's young democracy, noting that the transfer of power was taking place through constitutional means rather than force.

# Political Transition in South Africa, September 2008

## Background: The ANC Power Struggle

The events of September 2008 were the culmination of a bitter rivalry within the African National Congress (ANC) between President Thabo Mbeki and Jacob Zuma, his former deputy. This conflict had been building for years and reflected deeper ideological and factional divisions within the ruling party.

Mbeki had dismissed Zuma as Deputy President in 2005 after Zuma's financial advisor, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption and fraud in connection with an arms deal. Despite this dismissal, Zuma remained popular within the ANC's grassroots, labor unions, and the Communist Party, who viewed Mbeki as aloof and technocratic.

At the ANC's December 2007 conference in Polokwane, Zuma decisively defeated Mbeki for the party presidency, signaling a significant shift in power within the party even though Mbeki remained the country's president.

## The Corruption Case and Judge Nicholson's Ruling

The immediate trigger for Mbeki's departure came on **12 September 2008**, when Judge Chris Nicholson of the Pietermaritzburg High Court ruled that corruption charges against Zuma were invalid on procedural grounds. 

Crucially, Nicholson suggested there had been political interference in the National Prosecuting Authority's decision to charge Zuma, implying that Mbeki and members of his cabinet may have improperly influenced the prosecution. This ruling gave Zuma's supporters the ammunition they needed to move against Mbeki.

## Mbeki's Recall and Resignation

Following the Nicholson ruling, the ANC's National Executive Committee decided to "recall" Mbeki—effectively asking him to resign before the end of his term, which was due to conclude in 2009.

On **21 September 2008**, Mbeki announced his resignation in a televised address to the nation. He maintained his innocence regarding the allegations of interference in Zuma's case but stated he would comply with the party's decision, emphasizing his continued loyalty to the ANC and his commitment to a constitutional transfer of power. His formal resignation took effect on **25 September 2008**.

## Motlanthe's Appointment as Interim President

**Kgalema Motlanthe** was elected by Parliament and sworn in as President on **25 September 2008**. A respected figure and former trade unionist, Motlanthe had served as ANC Deputy President and was seen as a stabilizing, unifying choice for the interim period.

Key aspects of his caretaker presidency included:

- He was understood to be a transitional leader who would serve until the 2009 general elections, after which Zuma was widely expected to become president.
- His appointment reassured markets and international observers concerned about political instability.
- He retained many cabinet members, though some Mbeki allies, notably Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, briefly resigned before agreeing to stay on, which helped calm financial markets.

## Broader Significance

This transition was notable for several reasons:

- It marked the first time a South African president had been forced from office by his own party.
- Despite the drama, the transfer of power occurred constitutionally and peacefully, demonstrating the resilience of South Africa's democratic institutions just over a decade after the end of apartheid.
- The events deepened divisions in the ANC, leading a group of Mbeki supporters to break away and form a new party, the Congress of the People (COPE), in late 2008.

## Aftermath

Zuma's legal troubles continued, though charges were dropped in April 2009 shortly before the elections. Zuma led the ANC to victory in the **April 2009 general elections** and was inaugurated as President in May 2009, completing the transition that had begun with the September 2008 upheaval.

The Nicholson ruling itself was later overturned on appeal, with a higher court finding that the judge had overstepped his authority in making political inferences—but by then the political consequences had already reshaped South Africa's leadership.

## Ten Ministers and Deputy President Step Down in Political Crisis

**JOHANNESBURG** — South Africa's political landscape was thrown into upheaval today as ten cabinet ministers and the deputy president tendered their resignations in the wake of President Thabo Mbeki's departure from office, deepening a crisis within the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

The mass resignations came just days after Mbeki agreed to step down at the request of the ANC's National Executive Committee, which had recalled him from the presidency amid escalating internal party tensions.

## A Wave of Departures

Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka led the wave of resignations, joined by a group of senior ministers considered loyal to the outgoing president. The departures raised immediate concerns about continuity in government and stability in the country's leadership during a delicate transition period.

Political analysts noted that the resignations reflected deep divisions that had emerged within the ANC, splitting the party between factions aligned with Mbeki and those supporting his rivals.

## Mbeki's Farewell Address

In a nationally televised farewell address, Mbeki struck a measured and dignified tone, emphasizing his commitment to constitutional order and appealing for national unity.

"I have been a loyal member of the African National Congress for 52 years," Mbeki said. "I remain a member of the ANC and therefore respect its decisions."

The outgoing president sought to reassure citizens and investors alike, stating: "I would like to assure the nation that our beloved country will continue to grow and prosper."

Addressing speculation about the circumstances of his departure, Mbeki firmly denied allegations that had circulated in political circles. "I truly hope that this reality will manifest itself in practical ways in the days, weeks, months and years ahead," he said, reflecting on his hopes for the nation's future.

He added a note of personal reflection: "Gross insinuations have been made... I never sought to interfere in any legal processes. I have served to the best of my ability."

## Government Seeks to Reassure Public

Officials moved quickly to calm fears about the transition, emphasizing that the constitutional process would proceed smoothly. The ANC indicated that the National Assembly would convene to elect a new president to serve out the remainder of the term until scheduled national elections.

Party leadership pledged that essential government functions would continue uninterrupted, and that new appointments would be made to fill the vacant positions promptly.

## Economic Concerns

The resignations sent ripples through financial markets, with the currency experiencing volatility as investors weighed the implications of the political uncertainty. Economists cautioned that a prolonged period of instability could affect investor confidence, though many expressed hope that the constitutional transition would ultimately reassure markets.

## Looking Ahead

As South Africa navigates this pivotal moment, questions remain about the composition of the incoming administration and the direction of government policy. The transition marks one of the most significant political shifts in the country's post-apartheid history.

Observers will be watching closely to see whether the new leadership can heal the divisions within the ruling party and maintain the stability that has characterized South Africa's democracy.

# Thabo Mbeki's Resignation (September 2008)

## Background and Context

Thabo Mbeki's forced resignation stemmed from a bitter power struggle within the African National Congress (ANC) between Mbeki and his rival, **Jacob Zuma**. This rivalry had intensified after Mbeki dismissed Zuma as Deputy President in 2005 amid corruption allegations.

At the ANC's **December 2007 Polokwane conference**, Zuma defeated Mbeki for the position of ANC party president, creating a situation where the party leader and the country's president were different people—a significant political tension.

## The Trigger: The Zuma Case Dismissal

In **September 2008**, Judge Chris Nicholson dismissed the corruption case against Jacob Zuma. Critically, the judge's ruling suggested there had been **political interference** in the prosecution, implying that Mbeki's administration may have improperly influenced the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) to pursue charges against Zuma for political reasons.

## The Forced Resignation

Following this ruling:
- The ANC's National Executive Committee **"recalled" Mbeki**, effectively demanding his resignation
- Mbeki agreed to step down, resigning on **September 21, 2008**, though he denied interfering in Zuma's prosecution
- **Kgalema Motlanthe** was installed as caretaker president to serve until the 2009 elections

## Implications for South Africa

**Political consequences included:**
- **Party over state:** The events demonstrated the ANC's dominance, showing the party could remove a sitting president, raising concerns about the separation between party and state.
- **Cabinet resignations:** Several ministers resigned in solidarity with Mbeki, including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel (though he later returned), briefly rattling markets.
- **ANC split:** The turmoil led to a breakaway faction forming a new party, the **Congress of the People (COPE)**, in late 2008.
- **Zuma's rise:** The path was cleared for Zuma to become president after the 2009 elections.
- **Concerns about judicial independence:** The allegations of political interference in prosecutions raised questions about the health of South Africa's democratic institutions.

# South Africa at a Crossroads: Mbeki's Ouster Deepens Political Uncertainty

*A nation grapples with leadership turmoil as ANC infighting, legal controversies, and regional diplomacy converge*

---

**JOHANNESBURG** — South Africa is navigating one of the most turbulent political periods since the end of apartheid, as the governing African National Congress (ANC) moves to recall President Thabo Mbeki, a decision that has sent shockwaves through the nation's political establishment and raised questions about the stability of the continent's most developed economy.

## The Fall of a Technocrat

Thabo Mbeki, who succeeded Nelson Mandela in 1999, leaves behind a complex legacy. Widely regarded as a cerebral and technocratic leader, Mbeki presided over a period of sustained economic growth, with South Africa's GDP expanding steadily during much of his tenure. His government pursued fiscal discipline, attracted foreign investment, and oversaw the emergence of a growing black middle class.

Mbeki positioned himself as a champion of the "African Renaissance," advocating for the continent's self-reliance and playing an instrumental role in transforming the Organisation of African Unity into the African Union. He was a key architect of the New Partnership for Africa's Development (NEPAD), an ambitious framework aimed at eradicating poverty and promoting sustainable growth across the continent.

However, his presidency was not without significant controversy. Critics assailed his administration's slow and often contested response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic, with health policies that drew international condemnation. His perceived aloofness and centralization of power within the presidency also alienated many within the ANC's ranks.

## The ANC's Historic Decision

The immediate catalyst for Mbeki's downfall came from within his own party. Following the ANC's national conference in Polokwane in December 2007, where Mbeki lost the party presidency to his rival Jacob Zuma, tensions between the two power centers intensified.

The ANC's National Executive Committee ultimately took the extraordinary step of "recalling" Mbeki from the presidency—a move without precedent in the country's democratic history. While constitutionally the president is elected by parliament, the ANC's dominance means the party's decision effectively ends Mbeki's tenure ahead of the scheduled conclusion of his term.

The recall exposed deep fault lines within the liberation movement, pitting Mbeki's supporters against Zuma's populist coalition of trade unionists, communists, and youth activists who felt marginalized during Mbeki's rule.

## The Zuma Legal Saga

At the heart of the crisis lies the protracted legal battle surrounding Jacob Zuma, the ANC president and presumptive frontrunner to become South Africa's next head of state.

Zuma has faced a series of legal challenges, including corruption charges linked to a multi-billion-dollar arms deal. His former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of corruption in a case that implicated Zuma, fueling years of legal wrangling.

The situation reached a critical juncture when a High Court judge dismissed corruption charges against Zuma on procedural grounds. Significantly, the ruling contained remarks suggesting possible political interference in the prosecution—an implication that Mbeki's camp vigorously denied but which Zuma's supporters seized upon as vindication.

This judicial development provided the ANC with additional impetus to move against Mbeki, with Zuma's allies arguing that the former president had improperly influenced the judicial process against their leader.

## Mbeki's Zimbabwe Diplomacy

Even as his domestic authority crumbled, Mbeki remained engaged in one of the region's most pressing challenges: the political crisis in neighboring Zimbabwe.

As the designated mediator for the Southern African Development Community (SADC), Mbeki brokered a landmark power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai of the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC). The deal, reached after Zimbabwe's disputed and violence-marred elections, sought to establish a unity government to address the country's catastrophic economic collapse and political impasse.

Under the arrangement, Mugabe would retain the presidency while Tsvangirai would assume the newly created position of prime minister. The agreement was hailed by some as a diplomatic breakthrough, though critics argued that Mbeki's approach—often characterized as "quiet diplomacy"—had been too accommodating toward Mugabe and insufficiently forceful in confronting human rights abuses.

The timing was striking: Mbeki secured this regional achievement just as his own political fortunes were collapsing at home, underscoring the paradox of a leader more celebrated abroad than embraced by his own party.

## An Uncertain Path Forward

South Africa now faces a period of profound uncertainty. The transition raises critical questions about policy continuity, investor confidence, and the independence of state institutions. Financial markets have watched developments nervously, wary of any signals that could undermine the country's hard-won economic credibility.

The political drama also tests the resilience of South Africa's young democracy and constitutional order. Observers note that the peaceful, if contentious, transfer of power will serve as an important measure of the nation's institutional maturity.

As the ANC prepares for elections and the eventual ascension of Jacob Zuma, South Africans and the international community alike are watching closely to see whether the rainbow nation can weather this storm and preserve the democratic gains achieved since 1994.
